svg.title: A 10-month-old hospitalized for observation is in the playroom eating a teething biscuit when the caregiver calls out. The infant is clutching at his throat, has a weak, ineffective cough, makes no sound, and his lips are turning dusky. HR 150/min SpO2 88%
svg.desc: A weak, ineffective cough with no sound and clutching at the throat is the universal choking sign of a complete foreign body airway obstruction, not anaphylaxis, a breath-holding spell, or epiglottitis, none of which present this way. Back blows combined with chest thrusts is the correct maneuver for an infant (abdominal thrusts are reserved for children and adolescents), and a blind finger sweep is never performed because it can push the object deeper. Once breathing resumes the infant is placed side-lying with the knees bent for stability while the nurse trends respiratory effort and oxygen saturation to confirm the airway stays clear; temperature, urine output, lead level, and glucose have no bearing on this acute airway event.
